'''''Digitaria ciliaris''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by the common names '''southern crabgrass''',<ref name=usda>[http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=DICI ''Digitaria ciliaris''.] USDA Plants Profile.</ref> '''tropical finger-grass''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''tropical crabgrass''' or '''summer grass'''.<ref name=keys>[http://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/UQCentenary/key/UQ_Centenary/Media/Html/digitariaciliaris.htm ''Digitaria ciliaris'' - Common Australian Garden Weeds] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120502092638/http://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/UQCentenary/key/UQ_Centenary/Media/Html/digitariaciliaris.htm |date=2012-05-02 }}.</ref>

The grass is known as "ගුරු තණ - guru thana" in [[Sri Lanka]].

==Distribution and habitat==
''Digitaria ciliaris'' is a tough plant, believed to have originated in Asia but now found all over the [[tropical belt]] of the planet, as well as in many [[Temperate climate|temperate]] regions of both hemispheres.<ref name=cabi/> This grass is an [[invasive species]] considered an aggressive [[weed]] in certain countries, including [[China]], [[Mexico]] and the [[United States]].<ref name=cabi/>

This species has been observed growing in habitats such as coastal dunes, tidal marshes, and saw palmetto flats.<ref>Florida State University Robert K. Godfrey Herbarium database. URL: http://herbarium.bio.fsu.edu. Last accessed: May 2023. Collectors: Loran C. Anderson, A. F. Clewell, D. Crowson, D. S. Correll, R. K. Godfrey, Bruce Hansen, R. Komarek, R. Kral, H. Kurz, R. L. Lazor, Sidney McDaniel, Richard S. Mitchell, Paul Redfearn, William Reese, Ginny Vail, and Eula Whitehouse. States and counties: Florida: Bay, Collier, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Jackson, Leon, Liberty, Manatee, Okaloosa, Seminole, Taylor, Wakulla, and Walton.</ref>
  
Together with ''[[Portulaca oleracea]]'', ''[[Ipomoea pes-caprae]]'' and ''[[Wollastonia biflora]]'', ''Digitaria ciliaris'' is usually one of the first species colonizing [[Land degradation|degraded or altered environments]] in tropical zones of the planet.<ref>Heatwole, H., Done, T., Cameron, E. ''Community Ecology of a Coral Cay, A Study of One-Tree Island, Great Barrier Reef, Australia.'' Series: Monographiae Biologicae, Vol. 43, p. 102</ref>

==Description==
This grass is an [[annual plant]] that can grow up to 1 m tall but is usually much shorter. The roots are at the nodes and the stems produce [[stolon|runners]] that allow the plant to grow fast forming scruffy-looking patches about 1 m across and half a metre in height. The leaves are linear to linear-ovate narrowing at the tip to 15 centimeters long. The [[inflorescence]] is at the top of a long stem, usually much taller than the leaves, with two to nine  5–10 cm long sub-digitate racemes.<ref name=cabi>[http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/18912 ''Digitaria ciliaris'' - CABI]</ref>

==Forage Crop==
Southern crabgrass, and the related large crabgrass, especially the cultivars 'Red River Crabgrass', 'Impact', and 'Quick-n-Big', have been utilized as a forage crop for livestock, as it is a highly nutritious warm season grass.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://southeastagriseeds.com/blog-posts/crabgrass-short-step-weed-valuable-forage| title=Crabgrass: A Short Step from Weed to Valuable Forage!| author=Bouton, J.}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.johnstonseed.com/product/red-river-crabgrass/| title=Red River Fact Sheet}}</ref> Red river crabgrass responds well to nitrogen fertilizer, growing up to 3 feet tall, and needs to be in rotation with cool-season forage.
